content: Hello everyone! This is a follow up to my comment in the previous thread: I was wondering if people have had good experiences using agentic coding tools like Claude Code or Codex with Lean through VSCode or something similar. My experience with these tools for writing Python has been transformative, but I assumed they wouldn't have a strong training set on Lean and would perform badly so I kind of wrote them off. It seems like that might have been premature. I didn't see any posts on this question exactly, but reading through the history it seems like there has been a lot of work done having AI write entire proofs, which I want to clarify is not what I am asking about. I want to use it to augment my own work, not replace it.

Hi! I also have the same question! I have been using Lean+AI heavily for about a month, and here's my experience:

I have been able to fully one-shot certain simple (possibly novel) proofs using Codex (5.6 Sol Ultra on the plus plan).

I give it the pdf file (typeset with LaTeX) and then ask it to first formalize the theorems/lemmas/definitions. At the first pass, I ask it explicitly to only translate the theorems and not do any logic.
Then I check that these definitions/translations are correct. From there, I instruct it to strictly not modify/change these definitions from here on. Lemmas/Theorems go in a different file and I let AI have free will here. I don't use any specific skill.md file or anything, I just chat with the AI using Codex, ensuring that it is following my pdf file strictly and that all the intermediate steps make sense. Sometimes it tells me to change proofs slightly (e.g., instead of Pr[A | B] \leq c, prove Pr[A ^ B] \leq c * Pr[B], so that Pr[B] = 0 doesn't require extra casework etc.), and often I find it helpful.

Things to watch out for: Having hypothesis/definitions that hide the proof content and make lemmas/proofs trivial. Making no progress and reducing to a different lemma that essentially is the same as the original but more complicated to parse. From my experience, the blowup of LoC due to these issues is at least 5-6x, so it's not perfect, but appears to work! Also I've found it helpful to (re) write proofs having in mind that an AI is going to formalize it, and not a human. It helps to write definitions that are terse and use many qualifiers instead of subjective easy-to-read definitions that you will later have to fight with AI to formalize.

Disclaimer: I'm still a novice in lean, and I couldn't write a full proof from scratch without looking up documentation and in this case, I often get stuck on what commands do what ... etc.

Colin Bundschu said:

I assumed they wouldn't have a strong training set on Lean and would perform badly so I kind of wrote them off. It seems like that might have been premature.

Yes, this is premature, you are about 3 months out of date. Sol and Fable both write very good Lean code.

Srikkanth R said:

I give it the pdf file (typeset with LaTeX) and then ask it to first formalize the theorems/lemmas/definitions. At the first pass, I ask it explicitly to only translate the theorems and not do any logic.

Ok this is actually really similar to how I already work by hand, so I think it might carry over well. I have a python linter that enforces that every declaration in Lean maps back to a theorem or definition label exactly in the raw tex. The task of writing Lean becomes one of transcription. If anything isn't trivial to write in Lean (a felt degree of freedom or ambiguity), then I go back to the tex and break it down, then only go back to writing Lean when it feels unambiguous. The actual transcription step definitely feels like something AI could do.
